name: Togo
summary: A German colony, then a French mandate, independent in 1960; ruled by Gnassingbé Eyadéma (1967–2005) and then his son.

location.value: A narrow strip of West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea; 56,785 km².

terrain.value: A short coast with lagoons such as Lake Togo, a central plateau, the Togo Mountains running south-west to north-east, and northern savanna.

climate.value: Tropical: humid in the south with two rainy seasons, and drier savanna in the north with one rainy season.

resources.value: Phosphate rock near Lake Togo, fertile land for cotton, coffee and cocoa, limestone, and the deep-water harbour of Lomé.

disasters.value: Floods in the rainy season, such as the severe floods of 2007, droughts in the north, and erosion along the coast.

urbanisation.value: Largely rural, but Lomé, the capital and port, has grown to well over a million people; other towns include Sokodé and Kara.

disease.value: Malaria is the leading cause of illness; HIV, meningitis in the north and child malnutrition are also problems.

migration.value: Many Togolese work in Ghana, Nigeria and Benin; political unrest in 1993 and 2005 drove tens of thousands abroad as refugees.

economicBase.value: Farming of maize, cassava, cotton, coffee and cocoa, phosphate mining, and the port of Lomé, a hub for re-exports.

tradeRoutes.value: The deep-water Port of Lomé serves Togo and landlocked Burkina Faso, Niger and Mali; a coastal highway links Lagos and Abidjan.

wealth.value: A low-income country in which many people live in poverty, though Lomé’s port and services have grown.

moneyAndTax.value: The West African CFA franc, shared with neighbours and pegged to the euro.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A republic dominated by the Gnassingbé family since 1967; a 2024 constitution changed it to a parliamentary system.

keyRulers.value: Gnassingbé Eyadéma (took power in a coup on 13 January 1967; died 5 February 2005); Faure Gnassingbé (took office in February 2005).

succession.value: Faure Gnassingbé took office in February 2005 after parliament removed the clause requiring an election within 60 days; the African Union called it a military coup.

institutions.value: A National Assembly and courts; the 2024 constitution moved power from the president to a President of the Council of Ministers chosen by parliament.

stability.value: President Sylvanus Olympio was killed in a coup in January 1963; another coup followed in 1967, and protests in the 1990s and 2005 were put down.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The Togolese Armed Forces, recruited largely from the north, have been central to politics since the coups of 1963 and 1967.

majorWars.value: No major wars; violence has come mainly from coups and political unrest and, in the 2020s, from armed attacks in the far north.

territoryChange.value: British Togoland voted in 1956 to join the Gold Coast (Ghana); French Togoland became today’s Togo.

alliancesRivals.value: A member of ECOWAS (1975), the African Union and, since 2022, the Commonwealth; Lomé gave its name to the EEC’s Lomé Convention (1975).

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The University of Lomé (founded 1970) and the University of Kara (2004); French is the language of schooling.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: The port of Lomé, a north–south highway to Burkina Faso, a coastal road to Ghana and Benin, and the international airport at Lomé.

religion.value: A mix of Christians, Muslims (mostly in the north) and followers of traditional religions such as Vodun.

languageWriting.value: French is official; Ewe in the south and Kabiyè in the north are national languages, both written in the Latin alphabet.

artsArchitecture.value: The earthen tower-houses (takienta) of the Batammariba in Koutammakou, a UNESCO site (2004), and Ewe weaving, drumming and dance.

socialStructure.value: About 40 ethnic groups; the Ewe dominate the south and the Kabye the north, with long rivalry between them.

sharedIdentity.value: A national identity, though often divided between the south (Ewe) and the north, which has dominated the army and government.

dailyLife.value: People live in rural compounds or town houses; meals of fufu (pounded yam), maize paste (akoumé) and sauces with fish.

neighbours.value: Ghana to the west, Burkina Faso to the north and Benin to the east, with the Gulf of Guinea to the south.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity and Islam, with Vodun and other traditional religions still widely practised alongside them.

colonisation.value: German Togoland from 1884; divided into British and French mandates in 1922.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; phosphate earnings boomed briefly in the mid-1970s.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still in existence as an independent republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
